evidence.claim: Petersburg stands at the Appomattox River’s fall line, where Piedmont bedrock meets the coastal plain.
evidence.quote: Petersburg is located on the Appomattox River at the fall line, which marks the area where the Piedmont region (continental bedrock) and the Atlantic coastal plain (unconsolidated sediments) meet.

evidence.claim: The route’s historical thread is a struggle over movement and supplies.
evidence.quote: Union troops fought a series of battles with Confederate units, cut off or destroyed Confederate supplies and blocked their paths to the south and ultimately to the west.

evidence.claim: Union victories at Five Forks and Petersburg forced Lee to evacuate Petersburg and Richmond on the night of April 2–3, 1865.
evidence.quote: Union victories at the Battle of Five Forks on April 1, 1865, and the Third Battle of Petersburg, often called the Breakthrough at Petersburg, on April 2, 1865, opened Petersburg and Richmond to imminent capture. Lee ordered the evacuation of Confederate forces from both Petersburg and Richmond on the night of April 2–3

evidence.claim: He sought supplies at Farmville, but Union forces cut off the line of retreat at Sailor’s Creek on April 6.
evidence.quote: On April 6, 1865, Confederate General Robert E Lee’s Army of Northern Virginia wearily trudged its way through Amelia County in hopes of reaching greatly needed supplies at Farmville, Virginia. At Sailor’s Creek, Union General Ulysses S. Grant’s Union forces successfully cut off the line of retreat and attacked the rear guard.

evidence.claim: Three days later, Lee surrendered the Army of Northern Virginia to Grant at Appomattox Court House.
evidence.quote: the surrender of the Army of Northern Virginia under Robert E. Lee to Union commander Ulysses S. Grant took place on April 9, 1865

evidence.claim: High Bridge began as a Southside Railroad crossing in 1854, connecting Petersburg with Lynchburg over the Appomattox River.
evidence.quote: High Bridge was built by the Southside Railroad in 1854 to cross the Appomattox River and connect Petersburg with Lynchburg.

evidence.claim: On April 7, 1865, Confederate engineers set it on fire as Union troops approached.
evidence.quote: Confederate engineers succeeded in setting the bridge on fire on the morning of April 7, 1865, just as Union troops approached.

evidence.claim: Three wooden spans burned; Union engineers cut away a fourth burning span to stop the destruction.
evidence.quote: 3 of the bridge's 21 wooden spans had burned and a 4th span was on fire. Union engineers successfully cut the 4th span to prevent further destruction of the bridge.

evidence.claim: Rail traffic resumed that September after repairs.
evidence.quote: the South Side Rail Road company eventually finished the work and rail traffic resumed in September 1865.

evidence.claim: The last Norfolk Southern train crossed in 2004, and the company donated the abandoned line to Virginia in 2006.
evidence.quote: Norfolk Southern's last train crossed High Bridge on October 26, 2004, and in December 2006 the company donated 31 miles (50 km) of abandoned rail to the Virginia Department of Conservation and Recreation

evidence.claim: Restoration of the bridge completed the trail’s opening in April 2012.
evidence.quote: On April 6, 2012, after completion of the final segment of the trail, the restoration of the High Bridge itself, the trail opened for the first time for its full length

evidence.claim: Along the trail, telegraph poles and cement railroad mile markers remain.
evidence.quote: telegraph poles erected in the 1900s, remnants of the railroad's signal system, and Norfolk Southern's original cement mile markers.

evidence.quote: That day, Lee met with Grant to discuss terms of surrender at the McLean House. After discussion, Lee signed surrender terms that day, and on April 12, the Confederate Army of Northern Virginia laid down its arms and marched away.

flags: The cache’s List of Virginia Byways has no route entries, so the catalog’s March 20, 1995 designation and specific Virginia Byway status cannot be verified. The public copy identifies the NPS-supported driving tour instead.
The cache gives little present road geometry, landscape description or tour-development history and no whole-tour driving time; these gaps are not filled with campaign-era terrain descriptions.

The strip map runs eastward from Appomattox (mile 0) to Petersburg (mile 92.09). This story deliberately reverses it to follow the westward retreat; retained moments run Sailor’s Creek, High Bridge, Appomattox Court House. The NPS tour includes excursions beyond the strip corridor.
The 2015 NPS guide mentions AM 1610; no recent operational confirmation is supplied, so radio availability is omitted.
High Bridge height differs between NPS (160 feet) and Wikipedia (60–125 feet). Dimensions are omitted; the cache does not establish which original bridge components survive.

Sailor’s Creek casualty categories differ: Virginia State Parks says approximately 7,700 captured; NPS says 7,700 lost; Wikipedia includes other totals. Used the site manager’s qualified capture figure.
No motifs exist in the current story or retained moments; story motifs are empty and absent moment motifs are preserved.
